## Weak Convergence

::: {#def-aap-3-1 name="Weak Convergence"}

A sequence of distribution functions $F_n$ **converges weakly** to a
distribution function $F$, written $F_n\Rightarrow F$, if

$$
F_n(x)\to F(x)
\qquad\text{for every continuity point }x\text{ of }F.
$$

Equivalently, for distribution functions $F_n$ and $F$,

$$
F_n\Rightarrow F
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
F_n(x)\to F(x)\quad\text{for Lebesgue-a.e. }x\in\mathbb R.
$$


A sequence of random variables $X_n$ **converges in distribution** to $X$,
written $X_n\Rightarrow X$, if their distribution functions
$F_n(x)=\mathbb P(X_n\le x)$ converge weakly to that of $X$.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Why Only Continuity Points" collapse="true"}

Let $X$ have distribution function $F$ and set $X_n=X+1/n$. Then

$$
F_n(x)=\mathbb P(X+1/n\le x)=F(x-1/n)\to F(x-),
$$

the left limit of $F$ at $x$. So $F_n(x)\to F(x)$ only where $F$ is
continuous, even though $X_n\to X$ at every point of $\Omega$. Requiring
convergence at every $x$ would exclude this sequence.

\ 

More generally, if $X_n$ and $X$ are defined on a common probability space
and $X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)$ for $\mathbb P$-a.e. $\omega$, then $X_n$
**converges in distribution** to $X$:

$$
X_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}X
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
X_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}X
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
X_n\Rightarrow X.
$$

Here a.e. refers to $\mathbb P$ on $\Omega$, whereas the a.e. convergence
of distribution functions in @def-aap-3-1 refers to Lebesgue measure on
$\mathbb R$.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-3-1 name="Convergence in Probability and in Distribution"}

i) If $X_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}X$, then $X_n\Rightarrow X$.

ii) If $X_n\Rightarrow c$ for a constant $c$, then $X_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}c$.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

For (i), let $x$ be a continuity point of $F_X$ and fix $\epsilon>0$. Since
$\{X_n\le x\}\subseteq\{X\le x+\epsilon\}\cup\{|X_n-X|>\epsilon\}$,

$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty}F_n(x)\le F_X(x+\epsilon),
$$

and symmetrically $\liminf_{n\to\infty}F_n(x)\ge F_X(x-\epsilon)$. Letting
$\epsilon\downarrow0$ and using continuity of $F_X$ at $x$ gives
$F_n(x)\to F_X(x)$.

For (ii), the distribution function of $c$ is continuous at $c\pm\epsilon$
for every $\epsilon>0$, so

$$
\mathbb P(|X_n-c|>\epsilon)
\le F_n(c-\epsilon)+\bigl(1-F_n(c+\epsilon)\bigr)
\to 0+(1-1)=0.
$$

:::

::: {#thm-aap-3-3 name="Convergence of Expectations"}

$X_n\Rightarrow X_\infty$ if and only if

$$
\mathbb E\,g(X_n)\to\mathbb E\,g(X_\infty)
\qquad\text{for every bounded continuous }g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R.
$$

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

**($\Rightarrow$)** Let $U\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$ and set
$Y_n=F_n^{-1}(U):=\inf\{x:F_n(x)\ge U\}$. Then $Y_n\stackrel{d}{=}X_n$ and
$Y_n\to Y_\infty$ a.s. (Skorokhod's representation). For any bounded
continuous $g$, $g(Y_n)\to g(Y_\infty)$ a.s., so dominated convergence gives
$\mathbb E\,g(X_n)=\mathbb E\,g(Y_n)\to\mathbb E\,g(Y_\infty)=\mathbb E\,g(X_\infty)$.

**($\Leftarrow$)** Let $x$ be a continuity point of $F_{X_\infty}$ and
$\epsilon>0$. Sandwich $\mathbf 1_{(-\infty,x]}$ between continuous
piecewise-linear functions $g_{\epsilon,-}\le\mathbf 1_{(-\infty,x]}\le g_{\epsilon,+}$,
where $g_{\epsilon,+}$ drops linearly from $1$ to $0$ on $[x,x+\epsilon]$ and
$g_{\epsilon,-}$ drops on $[x-\epsilon,x]$. Passing to the limit gives

$$
F_{X_\infty}(x-\epsilon)
\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}F_n(x)
\le\limsup_{n\to\infty}F_n(x)
\le F_{X_\infty}(x+\epsilon),
$$

and letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ yields $F_n(x)\to F_{X_\infty}(x)$.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-3-4 name="Continuous Mapping Theorem"}

Let $g$ be measurable and let $D_g$ be the set of points at which $g$ is
discontinuous. If $X_n\Rightarrow X_\infty$ and $\mathbb P(X_\infty\in D_g)=0$,
then

$$
g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X_\infty).
$$

If in addition $g$ is bounded, then $\mathbb E\,g(X_n)\to\mathbb E\,g(X_\infty)$.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

Take the Skorokhod representation $Y_n\stackrel{d}{=}X_n$ with
$Y_n\to Y_\infty$ a.s. Since $\mathbb P(Y_\infty\in D_g)=\mathbb P(X_\infty\in D_g)=0$,
we have $g(Y_n)\to g(Y_\infty)$ a.s. By @thm-aap-3-1,
$g(Y_n)\Rightarrow g(Y_\infty)$, which is equivalent to
$g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X_\infty)$. If $g$ is bounded, dominated convergence
gives $\mathbb E\,g(X_n)=\mathbb E\,g(Y_n)\to\mathbb E\,g(Y_\infty)=\mathbb E\,g(X_\infty)$.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-3-6 name="Slutsky's Theorem"}

If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n\Rightarrow c$ for a constant $c$, then

$$
X_n+Y_n\Rightarrow X+c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
X_nY_n\Rightarrow cX.
$$

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

By @thm-aap-3-1(ii), $Y_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}c$. For any continuity point
$x$ of $F_{X+c}$ and $\epsilon>0$,

$$
\mathbb P(X_n+Y_n\le x)
\le\mathbb P(X_n+c\le x+\epsilon)+\mathbb P(|Y_n-c|>\epsilon),
$$

with a symmetric lower bound at $x-\epsilon$. Letting $n\to\infty$ then
$\epsilon\downarrow0$ gives $X_n+Y_n\Rightarrow X+c$.

For the product, write $X_nY_n=cX_n+(Y_n-c)X_n$. Since $X_n\Rightarrow X$ is
tight and $Y_n-c\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}0$, we have
$(Y_n-c)X_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}0$. Since $cX_n\Rightarrow cX$, the sum
case yields $X_nY_n\Rightarrow cX$.

:::

## Characteristic Functions

### Definition and Basic Properties

::: {#def-aap-3-3 name="Characteristic Function"}

The **characteristic function** of a random variable $X$ is

$$
\varphi(t)=\mathbb E\,e^{itX}=\mathbb E\cos(tX)+i\,\mathbb E\sin(tX),
\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
$$

:::

::: {#thm-aap-3-9 name="Properties of Characteristic Functions"}

Every characteristic function $\varphi$ satisfies:

i) $\varphi(0)=1$.

ii) $\varphi(-t)=\overline{\varphi(t)}$.

iii) $|\varphi(t)|\le1$.

iv) $\varphi$ is uniformly continuous on $\mathbb R$.

v) $\mathbb E\,e^{it(aX+b)}=e^{itb}\varphi(at)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-3-10 name="Characteristic Function of a Sum of Independent Random Variables"}

If $X_1$ and $X_2$ are independent with characteristic functions $\varphi_1$
and $\varphi_2$, then $X_1+X_2$ has characteristic function

$$
\varphi_{X_1+X_2}(t)=\varphi_1(t)\,\varphi_2(t).
$$

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Examples: Common Characteristic Functions" collapse="true"}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Coin flips, }\mathbb P(X=\pm1)=\tfrac12:&\quad \varphi(t)=\cos t\\
\text{Poisson}(\lambda):&\quad \varphi(t)=\exp\bigl(\lambda(e^{it}-1)\bigr)\\
\text{Normal}(\mu,\sigma^2):&\quad \varphi(t)=\exp\bigl(i\mu t-\sigma^2t^2/2\bigr)\\
\text{Uniform}(a,b):&\quad \varphi(t)=\frac{e^{itb}-e^{ita}}{it(b-a)}\\
\text{Exponential, density }\lambda e^{-\lambda x}:&\quad \varphi(t)=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-it}\\
\text{Cauchy, density }\frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)}:&\quad \varphi(t)=e^{-|t|}
\end{aligned}
$$

In particular, the standard normal distribution has $\varphi(t)=e^{-t^2/2}$.

:::

### Inversion and Continuity

::: {#thm-aap-3-11 name="Inversion Formula"}

Let $\varphi(t)=\int e^{itx}\,\mu(dx)$, where $\mu$ is a probability measure
on $\mathbb R$. If $a<b$, then

$$
\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-T}^{T}
\frac{e^{-ita}-e^{-itb}}{it}\,\varphi(t)\,dt
=\mu\bigl((a,b)\bigr)+\frac12\mu\bigl(\{a,b\}\bigr).
$$

In particular, the characteristic function determines the distribution: if
two probability measures have the same characteristic function, they are
equal.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

Since $\bigl|(e^{-ita}-e^{-itb})/(it)\bigr|=\bigl|\int_a^b e^{-ity}\,dy\bigr|\le b-a$,
Fubini's theorem exchanges the $t$- and $x$-integrals:

$$
\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-T}^{T}\frac{e^{-ita}-e^{-itb}}{it}\,\varphi(t)\,dt
=\int_{\mathbb R}R_T(x)\,\mu(dx),
$$

where
$R_T(x)=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^T\bigl(\frac{\sin(t(x-a))}{t}-\frac{\sin(t(x-b))}{t}\bigr)\,dt$.
By the Dirichlet integral $\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^T\frac{\sin(tu)}{t}\,dt=\tfrac12\operatorname{sgn}(u)$
(uniformly bounded in $T,u$), $R_T(x)\to\mathbf 1_{(a,b)}(x)+\tfrac12\mathbf 1_{\{a,b\}}(x)$
pointwise and boundedly, so dominated convergence gives the formula.

For uniqueness, $\mu$ has at most countably many atoms, so the formula
determines $\mu((a,b))$ for all non-atoms $a<b$ (a dense set). Letting
$a\to-\infty$ determines $F_\mu(b)$ on a dense set, hence everywhere by
[right-continuity on a dense set](1.qmd#cor-aap-1-5), which uniquely
determines $\mu$.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-3-12 name="Density from an Integrable Characteristic Function"}

If $\int|\varphi(t)|\,dt<\infty$, then $\mu$ has a bounded continuous density

$$
f(y)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-ity}\varphi(t)\,dt.
$$

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

Write $(e^{-ita}-e^{-itb})/(it)=\int_a^b e^{-ity}\,dy$. Since
$\int|\varphi(t)|\,dt<\infty$, we may send $T\to\infty$ directly in
@thm-aap-3-11 and apply Fubini's theorem to get

$$
\mu\bigl((a,b)\bigr)+\frac12\mu\bigl(\{a,b\}\bigr)=\int_a^b f(y)\,dy.
$$

The bound $|f(y)|\le\frac{1}{2\pi}\int|\varphi(t)|\,dt<\infty$ and dominated
convergence show that $f$ is bounded and continuous. Letting $b\downarrow a$
forces $\mu(\{a\})=0$ for every $a$, so $\mu((a,b))=\int_a^b f(y)\,dy$ for
all $a<b$, meaning $f$ is the density of $\mu$.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-3-13 name="Lévy's Continuity Theorem"}

Let $\mu_n$, $1\le n\le\infty$, be probability measures with characteristic
functions $\varphi_n$.

i) If $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu_\infty$, then $\varphi_n(t)\to\varphi_\infty(t)$
   for every $t$.

ii) If $\varphi_n(t)$ converges pointwise to a limit $\varphi(t)$ that is
    continuous at $0$, then the sequence $\mu_n$ is tight and converges
    weakly to the probability measure $\mu$ with characteristic function
    $\varphi$.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

Part (i) follows directly from @thm-aap-3-3 applied to $x\mapsto\cos(tx)$ and
$x\mapsto\sin(tx)$.

For (ii), Fubini's theorem and the bound
$1-\frac{\sin(ux)}{ux}\ge\tfrac12\mathbf 1_{\{|ux|>2\}}$ give, for every $u>0$,

$$
\mu_n\bigl(\{|x|>2/u\}\bigr)
\le\frac{1}{u}\int_{-u}^{u}\bigl(1-\varphi_n(t)\bigr)\,dt.
$$

Letting $n\to\infty$ by dominated convergence gives
$\limsup_n\mu_n(\{|x|>2/u\})\le\frac1u\int_{-u}^{u}(1-\varphi(t))\,dt$,
which tends to $0$ as $u\to0$ because $\varphi$ is continuous at $0$ with
$\varphi(0)=1$. Hence $\{\mu_n\}$ is tight.

By Helly's selection theorem and tightness, every subsequence of $\{\mu_n\}$
has a further subsequence converging weakly to some probability measure $\nu$.
By (i), $\nu$ has characteristic function $\varphi$, so by uniqueness
(@thm-aap-3-11) every subsequential limit is the same $\mu$; thus
$\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Why Continuity at 0 Is Needed" collapse="true"}

Let $\mu_n$ be the normal distribution with mean $0$ and variance $n$. Then

$$
\varphi_n(t)=e^{-nt^2/2}\to
\begin{cases}
1, & t=0,\\
0, & t\ne0,
\end{cases}
$$

which is not continuous at $0$. The sequence $\mu_n$ is not tight, since
$\mu_n\bigl((-\infty,x]\bigr)\to\tfrac12$ for every $x$, and it has no weak
limit.

:::

### Moments and Derivatives

::: {#thm-aap-3-17 name="Differentiation Under the Integral Sign"}

Let $(S,\mathcal S,\mu)$ be a measure space and $f:(a,b)\times S\to\mathbb C$.
Fix $y\in(a,b)$ and suppose there is $\delta>0$ such that on
$I=(y-\delta,y+\delta)\subseteq(a,b)$:

i) $f(t,\cdot)$ is integrable for every $t\in I$.

ii) $f(\cdot,x)$ is continuously differentiable on $I$ for every $x\in S$.

iii) $\partial_t f(t,\cdot)$ is integrable for every $t\in I$, and
     $v(t)=\int_S\partial_t f(t,x)\,\mu(dx)$ is continuous at $y$.

iv) The partial derivative satisfies

    $$
    \int_S\int_{y-\delta}^{y+\delta}|\partial_t f(t,x)|\,dt\,\mu(dx)<\infty.
    $$

Then $u(t)=\int_S f(t,x)\,\mu(dx)$ is differentiable at $y$ and

$$
u'(y)=\int_S\partial_t f(y,x)\,\mu(dx).
$$

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

The derivative is measurable in $x$ as a limit of difference quotients, and
continuity in $t$ gives joint measurability. The set on which
$G(x)=\int_I|\partial_t f(t,x)|\,dt$ is positive is $\sigma$-finite, since
each $\{G\ge 1/n\}$ has finite measure by (iv). By (ii), the derivative
vanishes on $I$ for every $x$ outside that set, so Fubini's theorem applies
on the $\sigma$-finite set.

For $0<|h|<\delta$, the fundamental theorem of calculus and Fubini's theorem give

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{u(y+h)-u(y)}{h}
&=\frac1h\int_S\int_y^{y+h}\partial_t f(t,x)\,dt\,\mu(dx)\\
&=\frac1h\int_y^{y+h}v(t)\,dt.
\end{aligned}
$$

By continuity at $y$, this average tends to $v(y)$ as $h\to0$.

For @thm-aap-3-14, take $f(t,x)=(ix)^ke^{itx}$ for $0\le k<n$. Its
derivative has absolute value $|x|^{k+1}$, which is integrable under the
moment assumption. This gives (iv) and, by dominated convergence, the
continuity of $v$ in (iii).

:::

::: {#thm-aap-3-14 name="Derivatives of a Characteristic Function"}

If $\int|x|^n\,\mu(dx)<\infty$, then $\varphi$ has a continuous derivative of
order $n$ given by

$$
\varphi^{(n)}(t)=\int(ix)^n e^{itx}\,\mu(dx).
$$

In particular, $\varphi^{(n)}(0)=i^n\,\mathbb E X^n$.

:::

::: {#lem-aap-3-1 name="Taylor Remainder Bound for Complex Exponentials"}

For every $x\in\mathbb R$ and integer $n\ge0$,

$$
\left|e^{ix}-\sum_{m=0}^n\frac{(ix)^m}{m!}\right|
\le\min\left(\frac{|x|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!},\,\frac{2|x|^n}{n!}\right).
$$

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

Integrating by parts gives, for every $k\ge0$,

$$
\int_0^x(x-s)^k e^{is}\,ds
=\frac{x^{k+1}}{k+1}+\frac{i}{k+1}\int_0^x(x-s)^{k+1}e^{is}\,ds.
$$

Starting from $e^{ix}-1=i\int_0^x e^{is}\,ds$, induction yields

$$
e^{ix}-\sum_{m=0}^n\frac{(ix)^m}{m!}
=\frac{i^{n+1}}{n!}\int_0^x(x-s)^n e^{is}\,ds.
$$

Using $|e^{is}|=1$ gives the bound $|x|^{n+1}/(n+1)!$. For the second bound,
$n=0$ follows from $|e^{ix}-1|\le2$; for $n\ge1$, rewriting the $(n-1)$-th
remainder as

$$
e^{ix}-\sum_{m=0}^n\frac{(ix)^m}{m!}
=\frac{i^n}{(n-1)!}\int_0^x(x-s)^{n-1}(e^{is}-1)\,ds
$$

and using $|e^{is}-1|\le2$ gives $2|x|^n/n!$.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Why the Integral Remainder Instead of Lagrange" collapse="true"}

For a complex-valued function $f=u+iv:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$, both the
**Peano remainder** and the **integral remainder** carry over verbatim by
applying the real result to $u$ and $v$ and forming $u+iv$: $o(x^n)+i\,o(x^n)=o(x^n)$,
and the two integrals share the same interval $[0,x]$.

The **Lagrange remainder** fails because the real and imaginary parts yield
different intermediate points $\xi_1\ne\xi_2$. Already for $n=0$ (the mean
value theorem), $f(t)=e^{it}$ has $f(2\pi)-f(0)=0$, yet $|f'(\xi)|=1$ for
every $\xi\in(0,2\pi)$.

| Remainder | Holds for $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$? | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Peano ($o(x^n)$) | Yes | $o(x^n)+i\,o(x^n)=o(x^n)$ |
| Integral | Yes | Same interval $[0,x]$; combines linearly |
| Lagrange | No | Real and imaginary parts need $\xi_1\ne\xi_2$ |

:::

::: {#thm-aap-3-15 name="Second-Order Expansion at 0"}

If $\mathbb E|X|^2<\infty$, then

$$
\varphi(t)=1+it\,\mathbb E X-\frac{t^2}{2}\,\mathbb E X^2+o(t^2)
\qquad\text{as }t\to0.
$$

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Two Proofs and Why the Explicit Bound Matters" collapse="true"}

By @thm-aap-3-14, $\varphi$ is twice continuously differentiable with
$\varphi(0)=1$, $\varphi'(0)=i\,\mathbb E X$, and $\varphi''(0)=-\mathbb E X^2$,
so a second-order Taylor expansion at $0$ gives the result immediately.

Alternatively, applying @lem-aap-3-1 with $n=2$ and $x=tX$ gives

$$
\frac{1}{t^2}\left|e^{itX}-\left(1+itX-\frac{t^2X^2}{2}\right)\right|
\le\min\left(\frac{|t|\,|X|^3}{6},\,X^2\right).
$$

As $t\to0$, the first bound tends to $0$ pointwise while the second provides
the integrable dominating function $X^2$, so dominated convergence yields the
expansion without differentiating $\varphi$. Unlike the qualitative $o(t^2)$
remainder, this explicit bound can also be summed uniformly across
non-identically distributed summands (such as triangular arrays).

:::

## Central Limit Theorems

### I.I.D. Sequences

::: {#thm-aap-3-16 name="Central Limit Theorem"}

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d. random variables with $\mathbb E X_i=\mu$ and
$\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2\in(0,\infty)$. If $S_n=X_1+\cdots+X_n$, then

$$
\frac{S_n-n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt n}\Rightarrow\chi
\qquad\text{as }n\to\infty,
$$

where $\chi$ has the standard normal distribution.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

Replacing $X_i$ by $X_i-\mu$, assume $\mu=0$. Let $\varphi$ be the
characteristic function of $X_1$. By @thm-aap-3-9 and @thm-aap-3-10,
$S_n/(\sigma\sqrt n)$ has characteristic function
$\varphi\bigl(t/(\sigma\sqrt n)\bigr)^n$, and by @thm-aap-3-15,

$$
\varphi\left(\frac{t}{\sigma\sqrt n}\right)^n
=\left(1-\frac{t^2}{2n}+o\left(\frac1n\right)\right)^n
\to e^{-t^2/2}.
$$

The limit is the characteristic function of the standard normal
distribution, so @thm-aap-3-13 gives the result.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example: De Moivre-Laplace Theorem" collapse="true"}

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d. with $\mathbb P(X_i=1)=\mathbb P(X_i=-1)=\tfrac12$,
so that $\mu=0$ and $\sigma^2=1$. For $a<b$, @thm-aap-3-16 gives

$$
\mathbb P\left(a\le\frac{S_n}{\sqrt n}\le b\right)
\to\int_a^b\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}\,dx.
$$

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example: Asymptotic Confidence Intervals" collapse="true"}

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d. with unknown mean $\mu$ and variance
$\sigma^2\in(0,\infty)$, and let $\bar X_n=S_n/n$. Given $\alpha\in(0,1)$,
choose $z_{\alpha/2}>0$ with $\Phi(z_{\alpha/2})=1-\alpha/2$ (for example,
$z_{0.025}\approx1.96$ for $1-\alpha=0.95$). By @thm-aap-3-16,

$$
\mathbb P\left(\mu\in\left[\bar X_n-z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n},\;
\bar X_n+z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\right]\right)
=\mathbb P\left(\left|\frac{\bar X_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\right|\le z_{\alpha/2}\right)
\to 1-\alpha.
$$

This random interval is an **asymptotic $(1-\alpha)$ confidence interval** for
$\mu$: the interval varies with the sample, while $\mu$ is fixed. When
$\sigma$ is unknown, replacing it by a consistent estimator $\hat\sigma_n$
(such as the sample standard deviation) preserves the same asymptotic
coverage by @thm-aap-3-6.

:::

### Triangular Arrays

::: {#thm-aap-3-18 name="Lindeberg–Feller Theorem"}

For each $n$, let $X_{n,m}$, $1\le m\le n$, be independent random variables
with $\mathbb E X_{n,m}=0$. Suppose:

i) $\displaystyle\sum_{m=1}^n\mathbb E X_{n,m}^2\to\sigma^2>0$.

ii) For every $\epsilon>0$,

    $$
    \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{m=1}^n
    \mathbb E\bigl[|X_{n,m}|^2\mathbf 1_{\{|X_{n,m}|>\epsilon\}}\bigr]=0.
    $$

Then $S_n=X_{n,1}+\cdots+X_{n,n}\Rightarrow\sigma\chi$ as $n\to\infty$, where
$\chi$ has the standard normal distribution.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

Let $\varphi_{n,m}(t)=\mathbb E\,e^{itX_{n,m}}$ and
$\sigma_{n,m}^2=\mathbb E X_{n,m}^2$. Applying @lem-aap-3-1 with $n=2$ and
splitting on $\{|X_{n,m}|\le\epsilon\}$ and $\{|X_{n,m}|>\epsilon\}$ gives

$$
\left|\varphi_{n,m}(t)-\left(1-\frac{t^2}{2}\sigma_{n,m}^2\right)\right|
\le\frac{|t|^3\epsilon}{6}\sigma_{n,m}^2
+t^2\,\mathbb E\bigl[|X_{n,m}|^2\mathbf 1_{\{|X_{n,m}|>\epsilon\}}\bigr].
$$

Summing over $m$ and letting $n\to\infty$ then $\epsilon\to0$ shows
$\sum_{m=1}^n\bigl|\varphi_{n,m}(t)-(1-\tfrac12 t^2\sigma_{n,m}^2)\bigr|\to0$.
Condition (ii) also implies $\max_{1\le m\le n}\sigma_{n,m}^2\to0$, so for
large $n$ all factors lie in the closed unit disk and
$\prod_{m=1}^n(1-\tfrac12 t^2\sigma_{n,m}^2)\to e^{-\sigma^2 t^2/2}$. Using
$\bigl|\prod_{m=1}^n z_m-\prod_{m=1}^n w_m\bigr|\le\sum_{m=1}^n|z_m-w_m|$
for $|z_m|,|w_m|\le1$ yields
$\varphi_{S_n}(t)=\prod_{m=1}^n\varphi_{n,m}(t)\to e^{-\sigma^2 t^2/2}$, and
@thm-aap-3-13 concludes the proof.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Recovering the I.I.D. Case" collapse="true"}

Let $Y_1,Y_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d. with $\mathbb E Y_i=0$ and
$\mathbb E Y_i^2=\sigma^2\in(0,\infty)$, and set $X_{n,m}=Y_m/\sqrt n$. Then
$\sum_{m=1}^n\mathbb E X_{n,m}^2=\sigma^2$, and

$$
\sum_{m=1}^n\mathbb E\bigl[|X_{n,m}|^2\mathbf 1_{\{|X_{n,m}|>\epsilon\}}\bigr]
=\mathbb E\bigl[Y_1^2\mathbf 1_{\{|Y_1|>\epsilon\sqrt n\}}\bigr]\to0
$$

by the dominated convergence theorem. Thus @thm-aap-3-18 contains @thm-aap-3-16.

:::

### Rates of Convergence

::: {#thm-aap-3-19 name="Berry–Esseen Theorem"}

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be i.i.d. with $\mathbb E X_i=0$,
$\mathbb E X_i^2=\sigma^2\in(0,\infty)$, and $\mathbb E|X_i|^3=\rho<\infty$. If
$F_n$ is the distribution function of $(X_1+\cdots+X_n)/(\sigma\sqrt n)$ and
$\Phi$ is the standard normal distribution function, then for every $x\in\mathbb R$
and $n\ge1$,

$$
|F_n(x)-\Phi(x)|\le\frac{3\rho}{\sigma^3\sqrt n}.
$$

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Why the 1/√n Rate Is Sharp" collapse="true"}

Take i.i.d. coin flips with $\mathbb P(X_i=\pm1)=\tfrac12$, so $\sigma=1$ and
$\rho=1$. When $n=2m$ is even, $F_n$ has a jump at $x=0$ of size

$$
\mathbb P(S_{2m}=0)=\binom{2m}{m}2^{-2m}\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi m}}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi n}},
$$

whereas $\Phi$ is continuous. Hence $\sup_x|F_n(x)-\Phi(x)|$ must be at least
half that jump, so the $n^{-1/2}$ rate cannot be improved in general. (The
constant $3$ is convenient for the proof; the best known universal constant
is below $0.4748$.)

:::
